source_description: Arthur O. Lovejoy manuscript notebook; faint front-leaf title ‘Symbolism’ [?]

batch.method: Manual visual correction against rendered PDF pages, using PaddleOCR-VL only as a scaffold.
policy: Preserve Lovejoy's argumentative distinctions and readable abbreviations.
Inserted slips are recorded as inserted notes rather than normalized into false pagination.
Do not silently normalize difficult ethnographic names, multilingual titles, or compressed bibliographic references.
Where handwriting is too poor for diplomatic transcription, retain only source-supported argumentative structure and mark uncertainties.

pages.corrected_text:
The page sketches a branching developmental relation among cultivated plants, domestic animals, and sacrifice and then turns explicitly against an assumed chronology. Direct-image control secures the objection that the proposed development 'involves a vicious circle.' The page challenges the premise that domestication universally precedes agriculture and records African counter-evidence that agriculture can be anterior to domestic animals and that domestic animals need not assist agricultural labor.

The economic/ethnographic premises are not Lovejoy-origin facts. The image-secure local operation is their use as an external chronological constraint on a proposed sacrificial genealogy.

pages.corrected_text:
The notes reject an automatic assumption that vegetation spirit/soul was originally conceived in human form and record animal or plant forms in the Mannhardt/Frazer comparative field.

A theory is then considered in which agrarian sacrifice consists in immolating the soul of the plant to itself so that the crop receives an equivalent/supplementary soul. The present summary allocates this theory toward a quasi-mechanical/magical mechanism rather than sacramental union, with a more complicated sacramental representative model treated as a different/later development. The constituent vegetation-spirit and mechanism categories are source-field material; exact Lovejoy-local allocation wording still requires diplomatic control.
